name: What Gear Actually Matters (A C-Tier vs. B-Tier Breakdown)
author: Printed by the Narrows Mutual Aid Press, compiled from community submissions
description: A practical equipment guide compiled by the Narrows Mutual Aid Press from anonymous community submissions, circulated in physical print through Shelf drop points and Narrows corner vendors. The zine targets C-tier freelancers looking to understand what gear is genuinely survival-critical versus what can wait until they have the Quanta to do it right. Includes contributor disagreements printed inline. Several sections show signs of heavy re-reading — pages 4 and 7 of the original are usually worn through on recovered copies.
body:
WHAT GEAR ACTUALLY MATTERS
A C-Tier vs. B-Tier Breakdown

Narrows Mutual Aid Press — Issue 14
Copy freely. Print on anything. Pass it forward.

---

This isn't for the person who just got their first payout and wants to feel like a freelancer. This is for the person who has Φ800 to their name, two jobs in the pipeline, and no idea where to spend it so they don't die on the third one.

We asked people who had been doing this for more than a year to tell us what they wish someone had told them. We got twenty-three responses. We cut the ones that were just bragging. What's left is below.

---

COMMS

C-TIER: Get a mesh-sync unit. Used. The gray-band ones off the Shelf markets are fine. You're not encrypting anything that matters yet — you don't have anything worth intercepting. What you need is reliable contact with your principal and, if you're running with anyone, line-of-sight relay capability. Spend Φ40–70. Don't spend more.

B-TIER: Once you're doing jobs where other people want to know what you're doing, you need layered encryption. Not because Arcturus is listening to every channel (they're not, they don't have to — they wait until after), but because rival freelancers and corporate counter-intel will absolutely harvest open channels for movement data. The Kurosawa-7 relay bands aren't cheap (Φ300+ used) but the encryption is genuine and the dead-channel fallback actually works. Do not buy anything that advertises "military-grade" on the packaging. That phrase means nothing and it usually means the vendor is counting on you not knowing that.

---

MEDKITS

C-TIER: The Shelf medpacks — the red ones, the ones that come in the foil wrapper — are adequate for what they are. Coagulant foam, two auto-inject adrenaline stabilizers, basic suture strip. They will keep you alive long enough to get to a clinic if you use them correctly. That's all they're supposed to do. The mistake people make is buying three of these thinking it equals one real medkit. It doesn't. Three coagulant foams won't close a through-and-through. Know what you have and plan your risk accordingly.

B-TIER: A full surgical field kit. The Veridian compact or equivalent. Costs around Φ600 new, Φ350–400 from a reliable used broker. Yes, it's heavy. Yes, you carry it. The difference between a Shelf foam pack and a full kit is the difference between "might survive" and "probably survives." The kit has an actual bio-reader, it administers correctly, it has clotting agents that work on augmented tissue. If you have chrome and you're using unmodified coagulants you are wasting your time and bleeding out faster than a baseline. This is the single most important upgrade you will make.

---

FOOTWEAR

Nobody talks about this. Everyone should talk about this.

C-TIER: Do not wear fashion. Do not wear construction surplus that was never designed for movement under load. You want a mid-ankle boot with a sole that can handle wet concrete, broken glass, and twelve hours of standing. The Durrant work series runs about Φ90 and it's worth every one of them. Resole them when the grip goes. Learn to resole them yourself — it's four hours of learning that saves you Φ60 every cycle.

B-TIER: If you're doing rooftop work, drainage tunnel runs, or anything that puts you in flood-adjacent zones (and in GLMZ that is almost everything east of the Shelf-7 stack), you want waterproof construction with a sealed ankle gasket. The Mitsubara Traverse series is the standard recommendation. Φ220 used, Φ400 new. People joke about spending freelancer money on boots. Those people have never done a six-hour extraction in ankle-deep runoff and then needed to sprint. Wet feet are a liability that compounds. Blisters turn into infections. Infections turn into missed jobs. Missed jobs turn into eviction.

Your feet are your primary system. Treat them like it.

---

WEAPONS: WHAT C-TIERS ACTUALLY CARRY VS. WHAT KILLS THEM

C-TIER reality: Most C-tiers are carrying whatever they could get — a short-barrel Praxis, a second-hand shock baton, maybe a folding blade. This is fine. This is workable. The problem is not the weapon, it's the misunderstanding of what the weapon is for.

A C-tier weapon is for getting away, not for fighting. If you are in a position where your Praxis is your plan, your plan has already failed. This sounds brutal but it will save your life more than any gear upgrade.

B-TIER: When you're moving up, the temptation is to buy the impressive thing. The long rifle. The plasma cutter modified for offensive use. Resist this. The B-tier upgrade that matters is reliability and adaptability — a weapon that handles non-standard ammunition, that has a realistic suppression option (not silenced, suppressed — know the difference), and that you have actually practiced with enough that it is not a surprise in your hands. A Φ900 weapon you've fired forty times beats a Φ3000 weapon you've fired twice.

[CONTRIBUTOR NOTE FROM "RATCHET," SHELF-9: I disagree with the suppressor call here. In my experience the acoustic signature on most B-tier jobs is less important than people say and suppressors add malfunction points. I've seen two people die because their suppressor assembly caught on a door frame. The important thing is the ammo versatility point, I'll give them that. But don't sink Φ200 into a suppressor kit before you sink it into a second clean magazine and three months of practice time.]

[ORIGINAL CONTRIBUTOR RESPONSE: Ratchet is not wrong that suppressors add failure points. Ratchet is also doing a lot of work in indoor corridors and not enough on open-floor industrial. Context matters. We'll leave both notes in.]

---

SHELTER GEAR

Because not every job ends cleanly, and because "sleep somewhere safe" stops being simple fast.

C-TIER: Emergency thermal wrap (Φ15, takes up no space, use it), a ground pad rated for wet surfaces, and the discipline to actually use them instead of pushing through exhaustion. Exhaustion is the enemy that doesn't look like an enemy until you make the mistake that ends you.

B-TIER: A compact shelter tent rated for the GLMZ eastern flood corridor environment. You need mold resistance, you need something that doesn't off-gas when wet, and you need setup time under three minutes. The Halloran Bivvy series is reliable. Φ180 used. Also: water filtration. Not the tablet kind for primary use — a gravity filter rated for industrial runoff. The tablet kind as backup. You will eventually be somewhere that the water situation is not clear and the difference between a filter and no filter is a week of illness you cannot afford.

---

BCI ADD-ONS: WORTH IT VS. GIMMICKS

This section only applies if you have a BCI. If you don't, skip to the end note.

C-TIER WORTH IT: A basic threat-overlay that reads biometric stress in your field of vision. Not combat prediction — that's aspirational and the cheap versions are worse than useless. Just stress read. Knowing that the person you're talking to is running high cortisol is basic social intelligence that pays for itself. Φ80–120 for a reliable used module.

C-TIER GIMMICK: Anything advertised as "reaction enhancement" under Φ500. The real reaction modules require calibration time and clean neural interfaces. The cheap ones create false-positive trigger responses and they have caused more friendly-fire incidents than Arcturus patrols in some districts. Leave them alone.

B-TIER WORTH IT: Encrypted memory partitioning. The ability to compartmentalize job data so that it isn't accessible under standard coercion-extraction protocols. This is not dramatic. This is not exciting. It means that if you get picked up and someone runs a basic pull on your BCI, the job details are not in the readable partition. Costs Φ400–600 depending on your hardware. It's not glamorous and it's saved more freelancers than any weapon upgrade on this list.

---

FINAL NOTE

Gear is not the job. Gear is infrastructure. The freelancers who die at C-tier mostly die because of decisions, not because of equipment gaps — but equipment gaps force bad decisions. That's the relationship. Spend on the things that expand your options. Save the rest.

Stay alive long enough to learn something.

— Narrows MAP, compiled with thanks to all contributors

Next issue: Medical augmentation and when to say no to the cheap clinic.
